edges.title: 独立成分分析的估计过程从根本上依赖于源信号的非高斯性。因为高斯变量在任何正交变换下都保持其分布不变，这导致无法唯一确定混合矩阵，因此非高斯性是成功分离独立成分的关键前提条件。

edges.to: 中心极限定理/Central Limit Theorem
edges.label: related_with
edges.title: 中心极限定理为非高斯性在独立成分分析中的重要性提供了理论支持。该定理指出，独立随机变量的总和趋向于高斯分布，这意味着通过最大化观测信号的非高斯性，可以有效地将其分解为原始的、更非高斯的独立成分。

edges.context: The Central Limit Theorem, a classical result in probability theory, tells that the distribution of a sum of independent random variables tends toward a Gaussian distribution, under certain conditions.

edges.label: related_with
edges.title: 峰度是衡量随机变量非高斯性的一种常用统计指标。它通过计算四阶累积量来度量概率分布的“尾部”厚度，其值偏离高斯分布的峰度（通常为0）的程度，可用于判断分布是超高斯还是亚高斯，从而量化其非高斯特性。

edges.title: 负熵被认为是衡量非高斯性的最优估计量。它通过比较一个给定随机变量的熵和一个具有相同方差的高斯变量的熵之间的差异来工作，负熵值越大，表明该变量的非高斯性越强。

slices.title: Lect.01
slices.text:
CS3308 机器学习

学习目标

- 能说出机器学习与其他领域区别和联系
- 会2-3种机器学习范式、及各自代表性模型、算法的思想、推导、实现、应用场景
- 了解机器学习的前沿技术与研究现状

教学方法

- 以课堂教学为主,结合阅读自学和大作业,进行分析和讨论
- Canvas平台直播+点播+讨论区(QQ)

教学安排

- 聚类分析
  - 层次聚类、k-mean、GMM
- 最大似然学习、EM算法
- 线性模型 (PCA, ICA, FA)
- 学习理论与模型选择
  - Bias-Variance, AIC, BIC, RPCL, Bayesian方法
- 因果发现
- 监督学习(线性回归、SVM)
- 神经网络 (感知机、BP算法)
- 深度学习
  - CNN, RNN, ResNet, DenseNet
  - AE, VAE, LMSER, GAN, Diffusion Model
  - 图神经网络: GCN/GNN
- 前沿专题
  - AlphaGo系列方法及应用

CS3308-机器学习-涂仕奎

第一章 机器学习 简介

教学内容 (要点)

掌握机器学习的基本概念, 对机器学习有概览性认识。

教学目标

课程目标1。

第七章 线性模型: FA

教学内容 (要点)

掌握PCA的产生式模型 FA, 以及相应的EM算法。

教学目标

课程目标2。

第二章 聚类分析: K-mean聚类

教学内容 (要点)

掌握机器学习建模的要点, 掌握 k-mean 聚类的建模过程、算法, 掌握竞争学习CL, FSCL, RPCL。

教学目标

课程目标2。

第八章 线性模型中的模型选择问题

教学内容 (要点)

掌握PCA的模型选择问题的求解方法, 并学会基本的、通过实验比较去研究和对比不同方法的优劣。

教学目标

课程目标2、3。

第三章 最大似然学习: GMM

教学内容 (要点)

掌握最大似然学习的建模要点, 掌握高斯混合模型 (GMM) 的建模过程, 比较 GMM 与 k-mean 的异同。

教学目标

课程目标2。

第十章 ICA的产生式模型

教学内容 (要点)

了解ICA的产生式模型, 并了解其与 FA、GMM 等的关系, 学会由简单组合得到复杂模型。

教学目标

课程目标2。

第四章 EM算

教学内容 (要点)

了解产生式模型, 掌握 EM 算法的基本原理, 学会基本的推导。

教学目标

课程目标1、2。

第十一章 神经网络: 感知机模型

教学内容 (要点)

掌握感知机模型的基本原理、及其局限。

教学目标

课程目标2。

机器学习的定义

- Arthur Samuel 的定义(1959)
  - 在不直接针对问题进行编程的情况下,赋予计算机学习能力的 一个研究领域。
- Tom Mitchell 的定义(1997)
  - "机器学习这门学科所关注的问题是:计算机程序如何随着经验积累自动提高性能。" (Machine Learning is the study of computer algorithms that improve automatically through experience.)
  - "对于某类任务T和性能度量P,如果一个计算机程序在T上以P 衡量的性能随着经验E而自我完善,那么我们称这个计算机程序 在从经验E学习。"

1.1 机器学习的定义

机器学习是一门人工智能的科学,该领域的主要研究对象是人工智能,特别是如何在经验学习中改善具体算法的性能。

机器学习是计算机系统利用算法和统计模型执行特定任务的科学研究，而不使用显式指令，而是依赖于模式和推理。它被视为人工智能的一个子集。机器学习算法基于样本数据（称为“训练数据”）构建数学模型，以便在没有明确编程执行任务的情况下做出预测或决策。机器学习算法广泛应用于电子邮件过滤和计算机视觉等各种应用中，在这些应用中，开发传统的算法来有效执行任务既困难又不可行。

机器学习与计算统计密切相关，计算统计侧重于使用计算机进行预测。数学优化的研究为机器学习领域提供了方法、理论和应用领域。数据挖掘是机器学习中的一个研究领域，侧重于通过无监督学习进行探索性数据分析。在其跨业务问题的应用中，机器学习也被称为预测分析。

What is Machine Learning?

Machine Learning (ML) is a fascinating field of Artificial Intelligence (AI) research and practice where we investigate how computer agents can improve their perception, cognition, and action with experience. Machine Learning is about machines improving from data, knowledge, experience, and interaction.

Machine Learning utilizes a variety of techniques to intelligently handle large and complex amounts of information build upon foundations in many disciplines, including statistics, knowledge representation, planning and control, databases, causal inference, computer systems, machine vision, and natural language processing.

AI agents with their core at Machine Learning aim at interacting with humans in a variety of ways, including providing estimates on phenomena, making recommendations for decisions, and being instructed and corrected.

In our Machine Learning Department, we study and research the theoretical foundations of the field of Machine Learning, as well as on the contributions to the general intelligence of the field of Artificial Intelligence. In addition to their theoretical education, all of our students, advised by faculty, get hands-on experience with complex real datasets.

Machine Learning can impact many applications relying on all sorts of data, basically any data that is recorded in computers, such as health data, scientific data, financial data, location data, weather data, energy data, etc.

机器学习与数据挖掘

"机器学习"是人工智能的核心研究领域之一,其最初的研究动机是为了让计算机系统的学习能力以便实现人工智能,因为众所周知,没有学习能力的系统很难被认为是具有智能。此前被广泛采用的机器学习的定义是"利用经验来改善计算机系统自身的性能"。事实上,由经验在计算机系统中主要是以数据的形式存在的,因此机器学习需要设法对数据进行分析,这使得它逐渐成为智能数据分析技术的创新源之一,并且为此而受到越来越多的关注。

"数据挖掘"和"知识发现"通常被相提并论,并在许多场合被认为是可以相互替代的。对数据挖掘有多种文字不同但含义接近的定义,例如"识别出巨量数据中有效的、新颖的、最终可理解的模式的非平凡过程"。其实顾名思于,数据挖掘就是试图从海量数据中发现有用的知识。大体上看,数据挖掘可以视为机器学习和数据库的交叉,它主要利用机器学习界提供的技术来分析海量数据,利用数据库界提供的技术来管理海量数据。

因为机器学习和数据挖掘有密切的联系,受主编之邀,本文把它们放在一起做一个粗浅的介绍。

基本术语-泛化能力 generalization

机器学习的目标是使得学到的模型能很好的适用于"新样本",而不仅仅是训练集合,我们称模型适用于新样本的能力为泛化(generalization)能力。

通常假设样本空间中的样本服从一个未知分布 D,样本从这个分布中独立获得,即"独立同视"(i.i.d)。一般而言训练样本越多越有可能通过学习获得强泛化能力的模型。

(色泽=?) $\land$ (根蒂=?) $\land$ (敲声=?) $\leftrightarrow$ 好瓜

在模型空间中搜索不违背训练集的假设 假设空间大小: 4*4*4+1=65

假设空间

目标与判断条件

- 目标：判断一个瓜是否为好瓜（好瓜和坏瓜，布尔类型）。
- 判断条件：假设好瓜可以由色泽、根蒂、敲声这三个属性完全确定。只需要通过这三个属性就可以判断出这个瓜是否是好瓜。
- 属性对应值：
  - 色泽: 青绿, 乌黑, 浅白
  - 根蒂: 硬挺, 稍蜷, 蜷缩
  - 敲声: 清脆, 浊响, 沉闷
- 特殊情况：
  - `*` 表示该属性所匹配所有结果，类似通配符，即该属性和判断瓜的好坏无关，取任意值都可以。
  - 不存在好瓜的情况用 `Ø` 表示。

假设空间的表示与计算

- 假设空间的表示形式为 "(色泽=?) ^ (根蒂=?) ^ (敲声=?)"
- 可以计算出共有 $4 \times 4 \times 4 + 1 = 65$ 种假设。

sample_triples.subject: 监督学习
sample_triples.description: 监督学习是机器学习的一个核心范式，其主要特点是利用一组已知类别的样本（即带有标签的训练数据）来调整分类器的参数，以达到所要求性能的过程。

sample_triples.subject: 聚类分析
sample_triples.description: 聚类分析是机器学习研究的一个重要方向，它属于无监督学习的范畴，旨在将数据集中的样本划分为若干个不相交的子集，每个子集称为一个“簇”。

sample_triples.subject: 深度学习
sample_triples.description: 深度学习是神经网络研究中的一个子领域，它特指使用包含多个隐藏层的深层神经网络结构进行学习的方法，旨在模拟人脑进行分析学习。

sample_triples.subject: 神经网络
sample_triples.description: 神经网络是机器学习的一个重要分支，它受人脑神经元结构的启发，通过构建包含多个处理层的人工网络来学习和表示复杂的非线性关系。

sample_triples.subject: K-均值聚类
sample_triples.description: K-均值聚类是聚类分析范畴内的一种代表性算法，具体属于非层次聚类方法，用于将数据集划分为预定数量（K个）的簇。

sample_triples.subject: 高斯混合模型
sample_triples.description: 高斯混合模型是一种基于概率模型的聚类方法，属于聚类分析的范畴，它假设数据点是由多个高斯分布的混合生成的。

sample_triples.subject: 高斯混合模型
sample_triples.description: 高斯混合模型的参数估计过程通常依赖于期望最大化算法，尤其是在存在未观测的隐变量（数据点所属的簇）时，EM算法提供了一种有效的迭代求解方法。

sample_triples.subject: 主成分分析
sample_triples.description: 主成分分析是一种经典的线性模型，主要用于数据降维，通过线性变换将原始数据投影到方差最大的新的正交坐标系上。

slices.title: Lect.04
slices.text:
Clustering: Models and Algorithms

Clustering the data

We want to cluster the data into two clusters (red and blue)

How?

Minimize the sum of square distances J

minimize
$$J = \sum_{n=1}^{N} \sum_{k=1}^{K} r_{nk} \|\mathbf{x}_n - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k\|^2$$

$r_{nk} = 1$ if and only if data point $\mathbf{x}_n$ is assigned to cluster k; otherwise $r_{nk} = 0$ .

k = 1, 2; K = 2 clusters

n = 1, ..., N;N: the total number of points.

We need to calculate { $r_{nk}$ } and { $\mu_k$ }.

If $J$ does not change, or ${ \mu_{1}, \mu_{2} }$ do not change, then the algorithm converges.

K均值法小结

- 初始化均值点 $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_k$
- 迭代如下
  - 把每个数据点按照就近原则分配给相应的 $\mu_i$
  - 把 $\mu_i$ 更新为所分配的数据点的均值
- 迭代停止, 如果聚类分配不变

Initialize $\boldsymbol{m}_i, i = 1, \dots, k$ , for example, to k random $\boldsymbol{x}^t$ Repeat For all $\boldsymbol{x}^t \in \mathcal{X}$ $b_i^t \leftarrow \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \|\boldsymbol{x}^t - \boldsymbol{m}_i\| = \min_j \|\boldsymbol{x}^t - \boldsymbol{m}_j\| \ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$ For all $\boldsymbol{m}_i, i = 1, \dots, k$ $\boldsymbol{m}_i \leftarrow \sum_t b_i^t \boldsymbol{x}^t / \sum_t b_i^t$ Until $\boldsymbol{m}_i$ converge

**Basic ingredients**

Model or structure

Objective function

Algorithm

Convergence
Questions

How many possible assignments for Kmean clustering?

Can K-mean algorithm always converge? Why?

Possible limitations of K-mean clustering?
Outline

Clustering

Adaptive learning (online learning) – CL, FSCL, RPCL

Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM)

Expectation-Maximization (EM) for maximum likelihood
**Hierarchical Clustering**

Agglomerative clustering

A very simple procedure:

Assign each data point into its own group

Repeat: look for the two closest groups and merge them into one group

Stop when all the data points are merged into a single cluster

**Hierarchical Clustering**

- Hierarchical clustering requires a measure of distance between *groups* of data points

**Distance** Measure

- Distance between data points a and b: $d(a, b)$
- Group A and B
  - Single-linkage $d(A,B) = \min_{a \in A, b \in B} d(a,b)$
  - Complete-linkage $d(A,B) = \max_{a \in A, b \in B} d(a,b)$
  - Average-linkage $d(A,B) = \frac{\sum_{a \in A, b \in B} d(a,b)}{|A| \cdot |B|}$

Clustering K-mean clustering, hierarchical clustering

Adaptive learning (online learning) – CL, FSCL, RPCL
Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM)
Expectation-Maximization (EM) for maximum likelihood

From batch to adaptive

Data points come one by one:

(a) $m_1$ is the winner
(b) $m_2$ is the winner

When starting with "bad initializations"

A four-cluster case

frequency sensitive competitive learning (FSCL) [Ahalt et al., 1990]
The idea is to penalize the frequent winners:
$$ \varepsilon_t(\theta_j) = \alpha_j \|x_t - m_j\|^2 $$

Rival penalized competitive learning (RPCL) (Xu, Krzyzak, & Oja, 1992, 1993)

The RPCL differs from FSCL by implementing $p_{i,t}$ as follows:

$$p_{j,t} = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } j = c, \ -\gamma, & \text{if } j = r, \ 0, & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases} \begin{cases} c = \arg \min_{j \in t}(\theta_j), \ r = \arg \min_{j \neq c} \varepsilon_t(\theta_j), \end{cases}$$

where $\gamma$ approximately takes a number between 0.05 and 0.1 for controlling the penalizing strength.

Rival penalized mechanism makes extra agents driven far away.

Questions

Are competitive learning (CL) and Kmean equivalent?

Could you come up with new algorithms to tackle the "bad initialization" problem of competitive learning (or K-mean)?

Can you design a K-mean version of RPCL?

Outline

- Clustering
  - K-mean clustering, hierarchical clustering
- Adaptive learning (online learning)
  - CL, FSCL, RPCL
- Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM)
- Expectation-Maximization (EM) for maximum likelihood

Issues for K-mean algorithm

Does it find the global optimum of J?

No, the nearest local optimum, depending on initialization.

- If Euclidean distance is not good for some data, do we have other choices?
- Can we assign each data point to the clusters probabilistically?
- If K (the total number of clusters) is unknown, can we estimate it from the data?
Probability distributions

• Read Bishop's PRML book, Chapter 2

Binary variables $x \in {0, 1}$

Bernoulli distribution

The probability of x = 1

$p(x = 1|\mu) = \mu$
$p(x = 0|\mu) = 1 - \mu$

$\operatorname{Bern}(x|\mu) = \mu^{x}(1-\mu)^{1-x}$

$\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[x] = \mu$
$\operatorname{var}[x] = \mu(1-\mu)$

Binary variables $x \in {0, 1}$

Bernoulli distribution

$\operatorname{Bern}(x|\mu) = \mu^x (1-\mu)^{1-x}$

Now suppose we have a data set $\mathcal{D} = {x_1, \ldots, x_N}$ of observed values of x. We can construct the likelihood function, which is a function of $\mu$, on the assumption that the observations are drawn independently from $p(x|\mu)$, so that

$p(\mathcal{D}|\mu) = \prod_{n=1}^{N} p(x_n|\mu) = \prod_{n=1}^{N} \mu^{x_n} (1-\mu)^{1-x_n}$.

$\ln p(\mathcal{D}|\mu) = \sum_{n=1}^{N} \ln p(x_n|\mu) = \sum_{n=1}^{N} \left{ x_n \ln \mu + (1-x_n) \ln(1-\mu) \right}$.

Multinomial variables

1-of-K scheme

$x_3 = 1$

$\sum_{k=1}^{K} x_k = 1$

Multinomial distribution

$p(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}) = \prod_{k=1}^{K} \mu_k^{x_k}$

$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{\mu} &= (\mu_1, \dots, \mu_K)^{\mathrm{T}} \quad \mu_k \geqslant 0 \ \sum_k \mu_k &= 1 \end{aligned}$

$\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}] = \sum_{\mathbf{x}} p(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu})\mathbf{x} = (\mu_1, \dots, \mu_M)^{\mathrm{T}} = \boldsymbol{\mu}$

$p(\mathcal{D}|\boldsymbol{\mu}) = \prod_{n=1}^{N} \prod_{k=1}^{K} \mu_k^{x_{nk}} = \prod_{k=1}^{K} \mu_k^{\left(\sum_n x_{nk}\right)} = \prod_{k=1}^{K} \mu_k^{m_k} \quad m_k = \sum_n x_{nk}$

$\operatorname{Mult}(m_1, m_2, \dots, m_K | \boldsymbol{\mu}, N) = \binom{N}{m_1 m_2 \dots m_K} \prod_{k=1}^{K} \mu_k^{m_k} \quad m_k = \sum_n x_{nk}$

Gaussian distribution

also known as the normal distribution

$$\mathcal{N}(x|\mu,\sigma^2) = \frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{1/2}} \exp\left{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(x-\mu)^2\right}$$

Multivariate Gaussian

$$\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{D/2}} \frac{1}{|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|^{1/2}} \exp\left{- \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\mathrm{T}} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\right}$$

The red curve shows the elliptical surface of constant probability density for a Gaussian in a two-dimensional space $\mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2)$ on which the density is $\exp(-1/2)$ of its value at $\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{\mu}$ . The major axes of the ellipse are defined by the eigenvectors $\mathbf{u}_i$ of the covariance matrix, with corresponding eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ .

$$\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}] = \boldsymbol{\mu}$$
$$\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{T}}] = \boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\mathrm{T}} + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}$$
$$\operatorname{cov}[\mathbf{x}] = \mathbb{E}\left[(\mathbf{x} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}])(\mathbf{x} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}])^{\mathrm{T}}\right]$$

Conditional probability

$$P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$$

The unconditional probability P(A) = 0.30 + 0.10 + 0.12 = 0.52.
The conditional probability $P(A|B_1) = 1$, $P(A|B_2) = 0.12 \div (0.12 \pm 0.04) = 0.75$, $P(A|B_3) = 0$.

Bayes Theorem

$$p(Y|X) = \frac{p(X|Y)p(Y)}{p(X)}$$

$$p(X) = \sum_{Y} p(X|Y)p(Y)$$

The Rules of Probability

Sum rule
$$p(X) = \sum_{Y} p(X, Y)$$

Product rule $p(X, Y) = p(Y|X)p(X)$.

More Distance Measures

Manhattan distance (city-block distance, L1 norm)
$$d_{fg} = \sum_{c} \left e_{fc} - e_{gc} \right $$

Euclidean distance (L2 norm)
$$d_{fg} = \sqrt{\sum_{c} (e_{fc} - e_{gc})^2}$$

Mahalanobis distance
$$d_{fg} = (e_f - e_g)' \Sigma^{-1} (e_f - e_g)$$, where $\Sigma$ is the (full or within-cluster) covariance matrix of the data

Pearson correlation (centered correlation)
$$d_{fg} = 1 - r_{fg}$$, with $r_{fg} = \frac{\sum_{c} (e_{fc} - \bar{e}_{f})(e_{gc} - \bar{e}_{g})}{\sqrt{\sum_{c} (e_{fc} - \bar{e}_{f})^{2} \sum_{c} (e_{gc} - \bar{e}_{g})^{2}}}$$

Uncentered correlation (angular separation, cosine angle)
$$d_{fg} = 1 - r_{fg}$$, with $r_{fg} = \frac{\sum_{c} e_{fc} e_{gc}}{\sqrt{\sum_{c} e_{fc}^2 \sum_{c} e_{gc}^2}}$$

$d_{fg}$ is the distance between expression patterns for genes f and g. $e_{gc}$ is the expression level of gene g under condition c.

sample_triples.description: K-均值聚类是一种具体的聚类算法，它在概念上属于聚类方法的一个重要分支，旨在将数据点划分到K个不同的簇中。

sample_triples.subject: 层次聚类
sample_triples.description: 层次聚类是一种具体的聚类算法，它在概念上属于聚类方法的一个重要分支，通过构建嵌套的簇的层次结构来对数据进行分组。

sample_triples.subject: 目标函数最小化
sample_triples.description: 最小化目标函数（即所有数据点到其所属簇中心的平方距离之和）是K-均值聚类算法的核心优化目标和工作原理。

sample_triples.subject: 收敛
sample_triples.description: 收敛是K-均值聚类算法的一个重要特性和终止条件，当目标函数J不再变化或簇中心不再更新时，算法达到收敛状态。

sample_triples.subject: 凝聚聚类
sample_triples.description: 凝聚聚类是层次聚类的一种实现方法，其特点是采用自底向上的策略，从每个数据点作为一个独立的簇开始，逐步合并最接近的簇。

sample_triples.subject: 距离度量
sample_triples.description: 距离度量是层次聚类算法的一个关键属性，用于定义和计算不同簇之间的距离，从而决定合并的顺序。常见的度量方法包括单链接、全链接和平均链接。

sample_triples.subject: 单链接
sample_triples.description: 单链接是在层次聚类中使用的一种具体的距离度量方法，它将两个簇之间的距离定义为两个簇中最近的两个数据点之间的距离。

sample_triples.subject: 全链接
sample_triples.description: 全链接是在层次聚类中使用的一种具体的距离度量方法，它将两个簇之间的距离定义为两个簇中最远的两个数据点之间的距离。

slices.title: Lect.05
slices.text:
Probability distributions

• Read Bishop's PRML book, Chapter 2

Binary variables

$x \in {0, 1}$

$0\leqslant\mu\leqslant 1$

Bernoulli distribution

The probability of $x = 1$

$p(x = 1|\mu) = \mu$

$p(x = 0|\mu) = 1 - \mu$

$\operatorname{Bern}(x|\mu) = \mu^{x}(1-\mu)^{1-x}$

$\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}[x] = \mu$

$\operatorname{var}[x] = \mu(1-\mu)$

Bernoulli distribution

$\operatorname{Bern}(x|\mu) = \mu^x (1-\mu)^{1-x}$

Let $\mathcal{D} = {x_1, \ldots, x_N}$ be a data set of observed values of x. The likelihood function, as a function of $\mu$, is constructed under the assumption that the observations are drawn independently from $p(x|\mu)$, so that

$p(\mathcal{D}|\mu) = \prod_{n=1}^{N} p(x_n|\mu) = \prod_{n=1}^{N} \mu^{x_n} (1-\mu)^{1-x_n}$.

$\ln p(\mathcal{D}|\mu) = \sum_{n=1}^{N} \ln p(x_n|\mu) = \sum_{n=1}^{N} \left{ x_n \ln \mu + (1-x_n) \ln(1-\mu) \right}$.

Multinomial variables

1-of-K scheme

$x_3 = 1$

$\sum_{k=1}^{K} x_k = 1$

Multinomial distribution

$p(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}) = \prod_{k=1}^{K} \mu_k^{x_k}$

$\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{\mu} &= (\mu_1, \dots, \mu_K)^{\mathrm{T}} \quad \mu_k \geqslant 0 \ \sum_k \mu_k &= 1 \end{aligned}$

$\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}] = \sum_{\mathbf{x}} p(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu})\mathbf{x} = (\mu_1, \dots, \mu_M)^{\mathrm{T}} = \boldsymbol{\mu}$

$p(\mathcal{D}|\boldsymbol{\mu}) = \prod_{n=1}^{N} \prod_{k=1}^{K} \mu_k^{x_{nk}} = \prod_{k=1}^{K} \mu_k^{\left(\sum_n x_{nk}\right)} = \prod_{k=1}^{K} \mu_k^{m_k} \quad m_k = \sum_n x_{nk}$

$\operatorname{Mult}(m_1, m_2, \dots, m_K | \boldsymbol{\mu}, N) = \binom{N}{m_1 m_2 \dots m_K} \prod_{k=1}^{K} \mu_k^{m_k} \quad m_k = \sum_n x_{nk}$

Gaussian distribution

also known as the normal distribution

$$ \mathcal{N}(x|\mu,\sigma^2) = \frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{1/2}} \exp\left{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(x-\mu)^2\right}
$$

Multivariate Gaussian

$$\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{D/2}} \frac{1}{|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|^{1/2}} \exp\left{-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\mathrm{T}} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\right}$$

$x_2$

The red curve shows the elliptical surface of constant probability density for a Gaussian in a two-dimensional space $\mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2)$ on which the density is $\exp(-1/2)$ of its value at $\mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{\mu}$ . The major axes of the ellipse are defined by the eigenvectors $\mathbf{u}_i$ of the covariance matrix, with corresponding eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ .

$$\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}] = \boldsymbol{\mu}$$
$$\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{T}}] = \boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\mathrm{T}} + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}$$
$$\operatorname{cov}[\mathbf{x}] = \mathbb{E}\left[(\mathbf{x} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}])(\mathbf{x} - \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}])^{\mathrm{T}}\right]$$

Conditional probability

The unconditional probability $P(A) = 0.30 + 0.10 + 0.12 = 0.52$.

The conditional probability $P(A|B_1) = 1$, $P(A|B_2) = 0.12 \div (0.12 + 0.04) = 0.75$, $P(A|B_3) = 0$.

Bayes Theorem

$$p(Y|X) = \frac{p(X|Y)p(Y)}{p(X)}$$

$$p(X) = \sum_{Y} p(X|Y)p(Y)$$

The Rules of Probability

sum rule
$$p(X) = \sum_{Y} p(X, Y)$$

product rule $p(X,Y) = p(Y|X)p(X)$.
Euclidean Distance

Distances at different directions could be different!

$$d(\vec{x}, \vec{y}) = \sqrt{(\vec{x} - \vec{y})^T \Sigma^{-1} (\vec{x} - \vec{y})}$$

$\Sigma$ is the covariance matrix

Probability

It is more powerful to consider everything in probability framework!

$$\frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^k |\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^{\mathrm{T}} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right)$$

Gaussian distribution with the Mahalanobis distance

$$D_M(x) = \sqrt{(x-\mu)^T \Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)}.$$

- Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM)
 - From generation process perspective

Issues for K-mean algorithm

Does it find the global optimum of J?

No, the nearest local optimum, depending on initialization.

- If Euclidean distance is not good for some data, do we have other choices?
- Can we assign each data point to the clusters probabilistically?
- If K (the total number of clusters) is unknown, can we estimate it from the data?

Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM)

Each cluster is represented as a Gaussian distribution $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_n \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)$.

$$\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}_{, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{, \boldsymbol{
u}}}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^{k} |\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^{\mathrm{T}} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right)$$

Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM)

We use $z_k = 1$ to indicate a point **x** belongs to cluster k

$$\mathbf{z} = (z_1, ..., z_K) \quad z_k \in {0, 1} \quad \sum_k z_k = 1$$

Assume the points in the same cluster follow a **Gaussian distribution**

$$p(\mathbf{x}|z_k = 1) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)$$

A mixing weight for each cluster:

$$p(z_k=1)=\pi_k \hspace{0.5cm} 0\leqslant \pi_k\leqslant 1 \hspace{0.5cm} \sum_{k=1}^{{\scriptscriptstyle K}} \pi_k=1$$

prior probability of point belonging to a cluster

So, we get a distribution for the data point **x**:

$$p(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{\mathbf{z}} p(\mathbf{z}) p(\mathbf{x} | \mathbf{z}) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x} | \boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)$$

Maximum likelihood

Given a data set $\mathbf{X} = (\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_N)^T$ in which the observations ${\mathbf{x}_n}$ are assumed to be drawn independently from a multivariate Gaussian distribution, we can estimate the parameters of the distribution by maximum likelihood. The log likelihood function is given by

$$\ln p(\mathbf{X}|\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = -\frac{ND}{2} \ln(2\pi) - \frac{N}{2} \ln |\boldsymbol{\Sigma}| - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{n=1}^{N} (\mathbf{x}_n - \boldsymbol{\mu})^{\mathrm{T}} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x}_n - \boldsymbol{\mu})$$

Maximizing the log-likelihood function:

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}} \ln p(\mathbf{X}|\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \sum_{n=1}^{N} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_n - \boldsymbol{\mu}) = 0 \qquad \longrightarrow \qquad \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{ML}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \mathbf{x}_n$$

Similarly we get $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{ML}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} (\mathbf{x}_n - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{ML}}) (\mathbf{x}_n - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathrm{ML}})^{\mathrm{T}}$

$\mu_{ML}$ and $\Sigma_{ML}$ are the maximum likelihood estimates of the mean and the co-variance matrix.

Matrix-cook-book

$\partial \mathbf{A} = 0$
$\partial(\alpha \mathbf{X}) = \alpha \partial \mathbf{X}$
$\partial (\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{Y}) = \partial \mathbf{X} + \partial \mathbf{Y}$
$\partial(\operatorname{Tr}(\mathbf{X})) = \operatorname{Tr}(\partial \mathbf{X})$
$\partial(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}) = (\partial \mathbf{X}) \mathbf{Y} + \mathbf{X} (\partial \mathbf{Y})$
$\partial (\mathbf{X} \circ \mathbf{Y}) = (\partial \mathbf{X}) \circ \mathbf{Y} + \mathbf{X} \circ (\partial \mathbf{Y})$
$\partial (\mathbf{X} \otimes \mathbf{Y}) = (\partial \mathbf{X}) \otimes \mathbf{Y} + \mathbf{X} \otimes (\partial \mathbf{Y})$
$\partial(\mathbf{X}^{-1}) = -\mathbf{X}^{-1}(\partial \mathbf{X}) \mathbf{X}^{-1}$
$\partial(\det(\mathbf{X})) = \det(\mathbf{X})\operatorname{Tr}(\mathbf{X}^{-1}\partial \mathbf{X})$
$\partial(\ln(\det(\mathbf{X}))) = \operatorname{Tr}(\mathbf{X}^{-1}\partial \mathbf{X})$
$\partial \mathbf{X}^T = (\partial \mathbf{X})^T$
$\partial \mathbf{X}^H = (\partial \mathbf{X})^H$

Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm for maximum likelihood

$$\ln p(\mathbf{X}|\boldsymbol{\pi}, \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \sum_{n=1}^{N} \ln \left{ \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_n | \boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k) \right}$$

E Step

When the parameters are given, the assignments of the points can be calculated by the posterior probability, i.e., the probability of a data point belonging to a cluster once we have observed the data point.

$$\gamma(z_{nk}) = \frac{\pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_n | \boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)}{\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^K \pi_j \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_n | \boldsymbol{\mu}_j, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)}$$

Soft assignment:

A point fractionally belongs to two clusters.

For example, 0.2 belong to cluster 1 0.8 belong to cluster 2

M Step

When the assignments $\gamma(z_{nk})$ of the points to the clusters are known, parameters could be calculated for each cluster (Gaussian) separately.

Mixing weight $\pi_k$: the proportion of number of points in cluster k within all data points

$$\pi_k = \frac{N_k}{N}$$ ; $N_k = \sum_{n=1}^N \gamma(z_{nk}).$

$\mu_k, \Sigma_k$: the mean and the covariance matrix are calculated for each cluster

$$\mu_k = \frac{1}{N_k} \sum_{n=1}^N \gamma(z_{nk}) \mathbf{x}_n$$

$$\Sigma_k = \frac{1}{N_k} \sum_{n=1}^N \gamma(z_{nk}) (\mathbf{x}_n - \mu_k) (\mathbf{x}_n - \mu_k)^{\mathrm{T}}$$

*L* denotes the number of cycles of the EM algorithm.

*L* denotes the number of cycles of E-Step and M-Step.

Summary for the EM algorithm for GMM

- Does it find the global optimum?
 - No, like K-means, EM only finds the nearest local optimum and the optimum depends on the initialization

- GMM is more general then K-means by considering mixing weights, covariance matrices, and soft assignments.

- Like K-means, it does not tell you the best K.

Discussion Question (1)

How can EM for GMM degenerate back to k-mean algorithm?

Generative process

- Generate $\mathbf{x}$ according to Gaussian distribution $p(\mathbf{x}|z_k = 1) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)$

So, we get a distribution for the data point $\mathbf{x}$:

$$p(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{\mathbf{z}} p(\mathbf{z}) p(\mathbf{x} | \mathbf{z}) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x} | \boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)$$

Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm for maximum likelihood

$
\ln p(\mathbf{X}|\boldsymbol{\pi}, \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \sum_{n=1}^{N} \ln \left{ \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_n | \boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k) \right}$

Initialization

Details of the EM Algorithm for GMM

1. Initialize the means $\boldsymbol{\mu}_k$, covariances $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k$ and mixing coefficients $\boldsymbol{\pi}_k$, and evaluate the initial value of the log likelihood.
2. E step. Evaluate the responsibilities using the current parameter values

$$ \gamma(z_{nk}) = \frac{\pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_n | \boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K \pi_j \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_n | \boldsymbol{\mu}_j, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)} $$

3. M step. Re-estimate the parameters using the current responsibilities

$$ \boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}^{\text{new}} = \frac{1}{N_{k}} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \gamma(z_{nk}) \mathbf{x}_{n} $$
$$ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k}^{\text{new}} = \frac{1}{N_{k}} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \gamma(z_{nk}) \left(\mathbf{x}_{n} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}^{\text{new}}\right)^{\text{T}} $$
$$ \boldsymbol{\pi}_{k}^{\text{new}} = \frac{N_{k}}{N} $$

where

$$ N_k = \sum_{n=1}^N \gamma(z_{nk}) $$

4. Evaluate the log likelihood

$$ \ln p(\mathbf{X}|\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma},\boldsymbol{\pi}) = \sum_{n=1}^{N} \ln \left{ \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_n | \boldsymbol{\mu}_k,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k) \right} $$

and check for convergence of either the parameters or the log likelihood. If the convergence criterion is not satisfied return to step 2.

The General EM Algorithm

Given a joint distribution $p(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Z}|\boldsymbol{\theta})$ over observed variables $\mathbf{X}$ and latent variables $\mathbf{Z}$, governed by parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, the goal is to maximize the likelihood function $p(\mathbf{X}|\boldsymbol{\theta})$ with respect to $\boldsymbol{\theta}$.

1. Choose an initial setting for the parameters $\theta^{\text{old}}$.
2. E step: Evaluate $p(\mathbf{Z}|\mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{old}})$.
3. M step: Evaluate $\theta^{\text{new}}$ given by

$$ \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\mathrm{new}} = \underset{\boldsymbol{\theta}}{\mathrm{argmax}} \mathcal{Q}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{old}}) $$

where

$$ \mathcal{Q}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{old}}) = \sum_{\mathbf{Z}} p(\mathbf{Z} | \mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{old}}) \ln p(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Z} | \boldsymbol{\theta}). $$

4. Check for convergence of either the log likelihood or the parameter values. If the convergence criterion is not satisfied, then let

$$ \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{old}} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{new}} $$

and return to step 2.

2. E step: Evaluate $p(\mathbf{Z}|\mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{old}})$.
3. M step: Evaluate $\theta^{\text{new}}$ given by

$$ \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{new}} = \underset{\boldsymbol{\theta}}{\mathrm{argmax}} \mathcal{Q}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{old}}) $$

where

$$ \mathcal{Q}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{old}}) = \sum_{\mathbf{Z}} p(\mathbf{Z}|\mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{old}}) \ln p(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Z}|\boldsymbol{\theta}) $$

Could you derive an EM algorithm for Bernoulli Mixture Model (BMM)?

$p(x = 1|\mu) = \mu \quad x \in {0, 1}$

$p(x = 0|\mu) = 1 - \mu \quad 0 \le \mu \le 1$

Bernoulli$(x|\mu) = \mu^x (1-\mu)^{1-x}$

Why EM never decreases the (log)likelihood?

EM never decreases the likelihood

Jensen's Inequality

For $\alpha_i \ge 0$, $\sum \alpha_i = 1$ and any {$x_i > 0$}
 $\log(\sum_i \alpha_i x_i) \ge \sum_i \alpha_i \log(x_i)$

Equality if and only if $\alpha_i = 1$ for some $i$ (and therefore all others are 0).

Mathematical background

The $\mathsf{KL}[q(x)||p(x)]$ is non-negative and zero iff $\forall x: \ p(x) = q(x)$

First let's consider discrete distributions; the Kullback-Liebler divergence is:

$$\mathsf{KL}[q||p] = \sum_i q_i \log \frac{q_i}{p_i}.$$

EM as maximizing a variational lower bound

Jensen's Inequality due to convexity

$\log(P(\mathbf{x}|\theta)) = \log(\sum_{\mathbf{y}} P(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}|\theta))$
$\log(P(\mathbf{x}|\theta)) = \log(\sum_{\mathbf{y}} q(\mathbf{y}) \frac{P(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}|\theta)}{q(\mathbf{y})})$
$\ge E_q[\log(\frac{P(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}|\theta)}{q(\mathbf{y})}]$
$\ge E_q[\log(\frac{P(\mathbf{x}|\theta)}{q(\mathbf{y})}]$
$\ge E_q[\log(P(\mathbf{x}|\theta)] - E_q[\log(\frac{q(\mathbf{y})}{P(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\theta)}]$
$\ge E_q[\log(P(\mathbf{x}|\theta))] - KL(q(\mathbf{y})||P(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\theta))$
$\ge \log(P(\mathbf{x}|\theta)) - KL(q(\mathbf{y})||P(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\theta))$
$\ge \log(P(\mathbf{x}|\theta)) - KL(q(\mathbf{y})||P(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x},\theta))$

$\ge E_q[\log(P(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}|\theta)] - E_q[\log(q(\mathbf{y}))]$

$\ge E_q[\log(P(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}|\theta)] + H(q(\mathbf{y}))$

An alternative view of EM

From wiki

Under some circumstances, it is convenient to view the EM algorithm as two alternating maximization steps.

$F(q, \theta) = E_{q}[\log L(\theta; x, Z)] + H(q) = -D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q \| p_{Z|X}(\cdot|x; \theta)) + \log L(\theta; x)$

where $q$ is an arbitrary probability distribution over the unobserved data $z$, $p_{Z|X}(\cdot |x;\theta)$ is the conditional distribution of the unobserved data given the observed data $x$, $H$ is the entropy and $D_{KL}$ is the Kullback–Leibler divergence.

Then the steps in the EM algorithm may be viewed as:

Expectation step: Choose $q$ to maximize $F$: $q^{(t)} = \arg \max_{q} F(q, \theta^{(t)})$

Maximization step: Choose $\theta$ to maximize $F$: $\theta^{(t+1)} = \arg \max_{\theta} F(q^{(t)}, \theta)$

Dirac delta function

The Dirac delta can be loosely thought of as a function on the real line which is zero everywhere except at the origin, where it is infinite,

$$ \delta(x) = \begin{cases} +\infty, & x=0 \ 0, & x \ne 0 \end{cases} $$

and which is also constrained to satisfy the identity

$$ \int_{-\infty}^\infty \delta(x)\,dx = 1 $$

This is merely a heuristic characterization. The Dirac delta is not a function in the traditional sense as no function defined on the real numbers has these properties. The Dirac delta function can be rigorously defined either as a distribution or as a measure.

A brief history of EM

EM had been "proposed many times in special circumstances" by earlier authors.
One of the earliest is the gene-counting method for estimating allele frequencies by Cedric Smith (1955).
A very detailed treatment of the EM method for exponential families was published by Rolf Sundberg in his thesis and several papers (1971,1974,1976).
The Dempster–Laird–Rubin paper in 1977 generalized the method and sketched a convergence analysis for a wider class of problems. The paper received an enthusiastic discussion at the Royal Statistical Society meeting with Sundberg calling the paper "brilliant".
The Dempster–Laird–Rubin algorithm was flawed and a correct convergence analysis was published by C. F. Jeff Wu in 1983.
Xu & Jordan in 1996 built up the mathematical connection between the EM and gradient-based approaches for maximum likelihood learning of GMM.

slices.title: Lect.06
slices.text:
Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM)

From generation process perspective

Expectation-Maximization (EM) for maximum likelihood

An alternative view to verify its properties

A brief history of EM

Instead if using ${\mu_{I_{j}}, \mu_{2}}$, each cluster is represented as a Gaussian distribution

$\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}_{, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{, \boldsymbol{
u}}}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^{k} |\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^{\mathrm{T}} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right)$

Introduce a latent variable

We use $z_k = 1$ to indicate a point **x** belongs to cluster k, $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, ..., z_K)$, $z_k \in {0, 1}$, $\sum_k z_k = 1$.

A mixing weight for each cluster:

$p(z_k=1)=\pi_k$

$0 \leqslant \pi_k \leqslant 1$, $\sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k=1$.

Prior probability of point belonging to a cluster:

$p(\mathbf{z}) = \prod_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k^{z_k}$

Assume the points in the same cluster follow a **Gaussian distribution**:

$p(\mathbf{x}|z_k = 1) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)$

Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM)

Generative process

- Randomly sample a $z$ from a categorical distribution $\pi = [\pi_1, ..., \pi_K]$;
- Generate $\mathbf{x}$ according to Gaussian distribution $p(\mathbf{x}|z_k = 1) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)$

So, we get a distribution for the data point $\mathbf{x}$:

$$p(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{\mathbf{z}} p(\mathbf{z}) p(\mathbf{x} | \mathbf{z}) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x} | \boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)$$

Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm for maximum likelihood

$$\ln p(\mathbf{X}|\boldsymbol{\pi}, \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \sum_{n=1}^{N} \ln \left{ \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_n | \boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k) \right}$$

Initialization

Details of the EM Algorithm for GMM

1. Initialize the means $\boldsymbol{\mu}_k$, covariances $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k$ and mixing coefficients $\boldsymbol{\pi}_k$, and evaluate the initial value of the log likelihood.
2. E step. Evaluate the responsibilities using the current parameter values

$$ \gamma(z_{nk}) = \frac{\pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_n | \boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K \pi_j \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_n | \boldsymbol{\mu}_j, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)}.$$

3. M step. Re-estimate the parameters using the current responsibilities

$$ \boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}^{\text{new}} = \frac{1}{N_{k}} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \gamma(z_{nk}) \mathbf{x}_{n} $$
$$ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{k}^{\text{new}} = \frac{1}{N_{k}} \sum_{n=1}^{N} \gamma(z_{nk}) (\mathbf{x}_{n} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}^{\text{new}})^{\text{T}} $$
$$ \boldsymbol{\pi}_{k}^{\text{new}} = \frac{N_{k}}{N} $$

where

$$ N_k = \sum_{n=1}^N \gamma(z_{nk}). $$

4. Evaluate the log likelihood

$$ \ln p(\mathbf{X}|\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma},\boldsymbol{\pi}) = \sum_{n=1}^{N} \ln \left{ \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_n | \boldsymbol{\mu}_k,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k) \right} $$

and check for convergence of either the parameters or the log likelihood. If the convergence criterion is not satisfied return to step 2.

The General EM Algorithm

Given a joint distribution $p(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Z}|\boldsymbol{\theta})$ over observed variables $\mathbf{X}$ and latent variables $\mathbf{Z}$ , governed by parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ , the goal is to maximize the likelihood function $p(\mathbf{X}|\boldsymbol{\theta})$ with respect to $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ .

1. Choose an initial setting for the parameters $\theta^{\text{old}}$ .
2. E step Evaluate $p(\mathbf{Z}|\mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{old}})$ .
3. M step Evaluate $\theta^{\text{new}}$ given by

$$ \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\mathrm{new}} = \mathrm{argmax}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{Q}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\mathrm{old}}) $$

where

$$ \mathcal{Q}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\mathrm{old}}) = \sum_{\mathbf{Z}} p(\mathbf{Z} | \mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\mathrm{old}}) \ln p(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Z} | \boldsymbol{\theta}) $$

4. Check for convergence of either the log likelihood or the parameter values. If the convergence criterion is not satisfied, then let

$$ \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\mathrm{old}} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\mathrm{new}} $$

and return to step 2.

2. E step Evaluate $p(\mathbf{Z}|\mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{old}})$ .
3. M step Evaluate $\theta^{\text{new}}$ given by

$$ \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\mathrm{new}} = \mathrm{argmax}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{Q}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\mathrm{old}}) $$

where

$$ \mathcal{Q}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\mathrm{old}}) = \sum_{\mathbf{Z}} p(\mathbf{Z}|\mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\mathrm{old}}) \ln p(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Z}|\boldsymbol{\theta}) $$

Could you derive an EM algorithm for Bernoulli Mixture Model (BMM)?

$\text{Bernoulli}(x|\mu) = \mu^x (1-\mu)^{1-x}$

Why EM never decreases the (log)likelihood?
EM never decreases the likelihood

Jensen's Inequality

For $\alpha_i \ge 0$, $\sum \alpha_i = 1$ and any {$x_i > 0$}
 $\log(\sum_i \alpha_i x_i) \ge \sum_i \alpha_i \log(x_i)$

Equality if and only if $\alpha_i = 1$ for some *i* (and therefore all others are 0).

Mathematical background

The $\mathsf{KL}[q(x)||p(x)]$ is non-negative and zero iff $\forall x: \ p(x) = q(x)$

First let's consider discrete distributions; the Kullback-Liebler divergence is:

$$\mathsf{KL}[q||p] = \sum_i q_i \log \frac{q_i}{p_i}.$$

To find the distribution q which minimizes $\mathbf{KL}[q||p]$ we add a Lagrange multiplier to enforce the normalization constraint:

$$E \text{ := } \mathbf{KL}[q \| p] + \lambda \left( 1 - \sum_{i} q_{i} \right) = \sum_{i} q_{i} \log \frac{q_{i}}{p_{i}} + \lambda \left( 1 - \sum_{i} q_{i} \right)$$

We then take partial derivatives and set to zero:

$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial q_i} = \log q_i - \log p_i + 1 - \lambda = 0 \Rightarrow q_i = p_i \exp(\lambda - 1)$$

$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial \lambda} = 1 - \sum_i q_i = 0 \Rightarrow \sum_i q_i = 1$$

Check that the curvature (Hessian) is positive (definite), corresponding to a minimum:

$$\frac{\partial^2 E}{\partial q_i \partial q_i} = \frac{1}{q_i} > 0, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 E}{\partial q_i \partial q_j} = 0,$$

showing that $q_i = p_i$ is a genuine minimum.

At the minimum is it easily verified that $\mathbf{KL}[p||p] = 0$ .

EM as maximizing a variational lower bound

Jensen's Inequality due to convexity

$$\log(P(\mathbf{x}|\theta)) = \log(\sum_{\mathbf{y}} P(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}|\theta)) $$
$$\log(P(\mathbf{x}|\theta)) = \log(\sum_{\mathbf{y}} q(\mathbf{y}) \frac{P(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}|\theta)}{q(\mathbf{y})}) $$
$$\geq E_q[\log(\frac{P(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}|\theta)}{q(\mathbf{y})}] $$
$$\geq E_q[\log(\frac{P(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}, \theta)P(\mathbf{x}|\theta)}{q(\mathbf{y})}] $$
$$\geq E_q[\log(P(\mathbf{x}|\theta))] - E_q[\log(\frac{q(\mathbf{y})}{P(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}, \theta)})] $$
$$\geq E_q[\log(P(\mathbf{x}|\theta))] - KL(q(\mathbf{y})||P(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}, \theta)) $$
$$\geq \log(P(\mathbf{x}|\theta)) - KL(q(\mathbf{y})||P(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}, \theta)) $$
$$\geq E_q[\log(P(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}|\theta)] - E_q[\log(q(\mathbf{y}))]$$
$$\geq E_q[\log(P(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}|\theta)] + H(q(\mathbf{y}))$$

An alternative view of EM

From wiki

Under some circumstances, it is convenient to view the EM algorithm as two alternating maximization steps.

Consider the function:

$$F(q, \theta) = \mathrm{E}_q[\log L(\theta;x,Z)] + H(q) = -D_{\mathrm{KL}}ig(qig\|p_{Z|X}(\cdot|x; \theta)ig) + \log L(\theta;x)$$

where *q* is an arbitrary probability distribution over the unobserved data *z*, $p_{Z|X}(\cdot |x;\theta)$ is the conditional distribution of the unobserved data given the observed data *x*, *H* is the entropy and $D_{KL}$ is the Kullback–Leibler divergence.

Then the steps in the EM algorithm may be viewed as:

Expectation step: Choose q to maximize F: $q^{(t)} = \arg \max_{q} F(q, \theta^{(t)})$
Maximization step: Choose $\theta$ to maximize F: $\theta^{(t+1)} = \arg \max_{\theta} F(q^{(t)}, \theta)$

Dirac delta function

The Dirac delta can be loosely thought of as a function on the real line which is zero everywhere except at the origin, where it is infinite,

$$ \delta(x) = \begin{cases} +\infty, & x=0 \ 0, & x \neq 0 \end{cases} $$

and which is also constrained to satisfy the identity

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(x)\,dx = 1. $$

This is merely a heuristic characterization. The Dirac delta is not a function in the traditional sense as no function defined on the real numbers has these properties. The Dirac delta function can be rigorously defined either as a distribution or as a measure.

A brief history of EM

- The EM algorithm was first proposed by Cedric Smith in 1955 for estimating allele frequencies.
- Rolf Sundberg provided a detailed treatment of the EM method for exponential families in 1971, 1974, and 1976.
- In 1977, Dempster, Laird, and Rubin generalized the method and provided a convergence analysis for a wider range of problems.
- C. F. Jeff Wu published a correct convergence analysis for the Dempster–Laird–Rubin algorithm in 1983.
- Xu & Jordan established the mathematical connection between the EM algorithm and gradient-based approaches for maximum likelihood learning of Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) in 1996.

The Dempster–Laird–Rubin paper in 19

Maximum Likelihood from Incomplete Data via the EM Algorithm

By A. P. DEMPSTER, N. M. LAIRD and D. B. RUBIN

Harvard University and Educational Testing Service

A broadly applicable algorithm for computing maximum likelihood estimates from incomplete data is presented at various levels of generality. Theory showing the monotone behaviour of the likelihood and convergence of the algorithm is derived. Many examples are sketched, including missing value situations, applications to grouped, censored or truncated data, finite mixture models, variance component estimation, hyperparameter estimation, iteratively reweighted least squares and factor analysis.

Keywords: MAXIMUM LIKELIHOOD; INCOMPLETE DATA; EM ALGORITHM; POSTERIOR MODE

..

On Convergence Properties of the EM Algorithm for Gaussian Mixtures

We build up the mathematical connection between the "Expectation-Maximization" (EM) algorithm and gradient-based approaches for maximum likelihood learning of finite gaussian mixtures. We show that the EM step in parameter space is obtained from the gradient via a projection matrix P, and we provide an explicit expression for the matrix. We then analyze the convergence of EM in terms of special properties of P and provide new results analyzing the effect that P has on the likelihood surface. Based on these mathematical results, we present a comparative discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of EM and other algorithms for the learning of gaussian mixture models. EM has a number of properties that make it a particularly attractive algorithm for mixture models. It enjoys automatic satisfaction of probabilistic constraints, monotonic convergence without the need to set a learning rate, and low computational overhead. Although EM has the reputation of being a slow algorithm, we feel that in the mixture setting the slowness of EM has been overstated. Although EM can indeed converge slowly for problems in which the mixture components are not well separated, the Hessian is poorly conditioned for such problems and thus other gradient-based algorithms (including Newton's method) are also likely to perform poorly. Moreover, if one's concern is convergence in likelihood, then EM generally performs well even for these illconditioned problems. Indeed the algorithm provides a certain amount of safety in such cases, despite the poor conditioning. It is also important to emphasize that the case of poorly separated mixture components can be viewed as a problem in model selection (too many mixture components are being included in the model), and should be handled by regularization techniques.

The fact that EM is a first-order algorithm certainly implies that EM is no panacea, but does not imply that EM has no advantages over gradient ascent or superlinear methods. First, it is important to appreciate that convergence rate results are generally obtained for unconstrained optimization, and are not necessarily indicative of performance on constrained optimization problems. Also, as we have demonstrated, there are conditions under which the condition number of the effective Hessian of the EM algorithm tends toward one, showing that EM can approximate a superlinear method. Finally, in cases of a poorly conditioned Hessian, superlinear convergence is not necessarily a virtue. In such cases many optimization schemes, including EM, essentially revert to gradient ascent.

sample_triples.subject: 期望步骤
sample_triples.description: 期望步骤是期望最大化（EM）算法的两个核心组成部分之一，此步骤主要负责在给定当前模型参数的情况下，计算关于隐变量的期望。

sample_triples.subject: 最大化步骤
sample_triples.description: 最大化步骤是期望最大化（EM）算法的两个核心组成部分之一，此步骤负责基于期望步骤的结果，通过最大化某个函数来更新模型参数。

sample_triples.subject: 最大化步骤
sample_triples.description: 在期望最大化（EM）算法的迭代流程中，最大化步骤的执行依赖于期望步骤的计算结果（如后验概率分布q^(t)），利用该结果来优化模型参数。

sample_triples.subject: 后验概率计算
sample_triples.description: 在期望步骤（E-step）中，其核心任务是评估或计算在给定观测数据和当前参数下，隐变量的后验概率分布。

sample_triples.subject: Q函数最大化
sample_triples.description: 在最大化步骤（M-step）中，其核心任务是通过最大化Q函数（对数似然函数在E步后验概率下的期望）来求解新的模型参数。

sample_triples.subject: 狄拉克δ函数
sample_triples.description: 狄拉克δ函数在数学上不被视为传统意义上的函数，而是一种广义函数，可以被严格地定义为一种分布。

sample_triples.subject: 积分为一
sample_triples.description: 积分为一是狄拉克δ函数的一个基本约束属性，即该函数在整个实数域上的积分值必须等于1。

sample_triples.subject: E步
sample_triples.description: E步（期望步）是期望最大化算法的两个核心迭代步骤之一，其主要任务是在给定当前模型参数的条件下，计算隐藏变量的期望（或后验概率分布），为M步的参数更新提供基础。

slices.title: Lect.07
slices.text:
Bayesian Learning

Bayes rule

$$P(\Theta|X) = \frac{P(X|\Theta)P(\Theta)}{P(X)}$$

$P(X|\Theta)$ : likelihood of data $X$ given parameter $\Theta$ $P(\Theta)$ : prior distribution over the parameter $\Theta$ $P(X)$ : marginal distribution of data $X$

- Prior distribution
  - Represents expert knowledge
- Uninformative priors: Uniform distribution
- Conjugate priors: Closed-form representation of posterior, $P(\theta)$ and $P(\theta|D)$ have the same form

Maximum A Posteriori (MAP)

$\max_{\Theta} p(\Theta|X)$

Equivalent to:

$\log p(X, \Theta) = \log p(X | \Theta) + \log p(\Theta)$

Consider a simple example:

$p(x|\Theta) = G(x|\mu, \Sigma)$
$p(\mu) = G(\mu|\mu_0, \sigma_0^2)$

When is MAP the same as MLE?

Maximum Likelihood estimation (MLE)
Choose value that maximizes the probability of observed data

$\hat{\theta}_{MLE} = \arg\max_{\theta} P(D|\theta)$

Maximum *a posteriori* (MAP) estimation

Choose value that is most probable given observed data and prior belief

$\widehat{\theta}_{MAP} = \arg \max_{\theta} P(\theta|D)$

$= \arg \max_{\theta} P(D|\theta)P(\theta)$

Model selection for generalization

Probabilistic model $p(X_N \mid \Theta_K)$

Criterion

Candidate models: $\Theta_1 \subseteq \Theta_2 \subseteq \cdots \subseteq \Theta_K \subseteq \cdots $

A trade-off between fitting the data well and keeping the model simple

Models become more and more complex as K increases.

Negative loglikelihood (or fitting error) to make sure the model fit the data well.

$d_k$ : number of free parameters N: sample size

Akaike's Information Criterion (AIC)

Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC)

da $\ln p(X_N \mid \hat{\Theta}_K) - d_k$ $\ln p(X_N \mid \hat{\Theta}_K) - \frac{1}{2} d_k \ln N$

Two-phase method for model selection

- Assume the optimal $K^*$ is within the range $[1, K_{max}]$ .
- Phase (1): For each $k = 1, ..., K_{max}$ , compute the maximum likelihood estimator:

$\widehat{\Theta}_{ML}(k) = \arg\max_{\Theta} \log[P(X|\Theta, k)]$

Phase (2): Select the optimal K* by optimizing the values of the model selection criterion J, e.g., AIC, BIC:

$$K^* = \operatorname{argmax}_k J(\widehat{\Theta}_{ML}(k))$$
Akaike's Information Criterion (AIC) $\ln p(X_N \mid \hat{\Theta}_K) - d_k$

Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) $\ln p(X_N \mid \hat{\Theta}_K) - \frac{1}{2} d_k \ln N$

Model selection

Probabilistic model $p(X_N \mid \Theta_K)$

Candidate models: $\Theta_1 \subseteq \Theta_2 \subseteq \cdots \subseteq \Theta_K \subseteq \cdots$

Compare model classes m using their posterior probability given the data:

$$P(m|\mathbf{y}) = \frac{P(\mathbf{y}|m)P(m)}{P(\mathbf{y})}, \qquad P(\mathbf{y}|m) = \int_{\Theta_m} P(\mathbf{y}|\boldsymbol{\theta}_m, m)P(\boldsymbol{\theta}_m|m) \ d\boldsymbol{\theta}_m$$

Interpretation of $P(\mathbf{y}|m)$ : The probability that *randomly selected* parameter values from the model class would generate data set $\mathbf{y}$ .

Model classes that are too simple are unlikely to generate the data set.

Model classes that are too complex can generate many possible data sets, so again, they are unlikely to generate that particular data set at random.

Bayesian model selection

A model class $m$ is a set of models parameterized by $\theta_m$, e.g., the set of all possible mixtures of $m$ Gaussians.
The marginal likelihood of model class $m$:

$$P(\mathbf{y}|m) = \int_{\Theta_m} P(\mathbf{y}|\boldsymbol{\theta}_m, m) P(\boldsymbol{\theta}_m|m) \ d\boldsymbol{\theta}_m$$
is also known as the Bayesian evidence for model $m$.
The ratio of two marginal likelihoods is known as the Bayes factor:

$$\frac{P(\mathbf{y}|m)}{P(\mathbf{y}|m')}$$
The Occam's Razor principle is, roughly speaking, that one should prefer simpler explanations than more complex explanations.
Bayesian inference formalizes and *automatically* implements the Occam's Razor principle.

VBEM for GMM

Model descriptions

$$p(\mathbf{Z}|\boldsymbol{\pi}) = \prod_{n=1}^{N} \prod_{k=1}^{K} \pi_{k}^{z_{nk}} \quad p(\mathbf{X}|\mathbf{Z}, \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Lambda}) = \prod_{n=1}^{N} \prod_{k=1}^{K} \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{x}_{n} | \boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}, \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{k}^{-1}\right)^{z_{nk}}$$

Prior distributions over parameters

$$p(\boldsymbol{\pi}) = \operatorname{Dir}(\boldsymbol{\pi}|\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{0}) = C(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{0}) \prod_{k=1}^{K} \pi_{k}^{\alpha_{0}-1}$$
$$p(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Lambda}) = p(\boldsymbol{\mu}|\boldsymbol{\Lambda})p(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})$$
$$= \prod_{k=1}^{K} \mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{k}|\mathbf{m}_{0}, (\beta_{0}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{k})^{-1}\right) \mathcal{W}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{k}|\mathbf{W}_{0},
u_{0})$$

$p(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Z}, \boldsymbol{\pi}, \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Lambda}) = p(\mathbf{X} | \mathbf{Z}, \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Lambda}) p(\mathbf{Z} | \boldsymbol{\pi}) p(\boldsymbol{\pi}) p(\boldsymbol{\mu} | \boldsymbol{\Lambda}) p(\boldsymbol{\Lambda})$$

sample_triples.subject: 贝叶斯学习
sample_triples.description: 贝叶斯学习是一种基于贝叶斯定理的统计推断框架，它通过应用贝叶斯定理来结合先验知识和数据证据，从而更新对未知参数的信念。

sample_triples.subject: 后验分布
sample_triples.description: 后验分布的计算完全依赖于贝叶斯定理，该定理明确了后验分布与似然、先验分布以及边缘分布之间的数学关系。

sample_triples.subject: 似然
sample_triples.description: 似然是贝叶斯定理公式中的一个核心组成部分，它量化了在给定参数下观测到特定数据的可能性。

sample_triples.subject: 先验分布
sample_triples.description: 先验分布是贝叶斯定理公式中的另一个核心组成部分，它代表在观测到任何数据之前，我们对参数的已有知识或信念。

sample_triples.subject: 无信息先验
sample_triples.description: 无信息先验是先验分布的一种具体类型，通常在缺乏关于参数的明确专家知识时被选用，例如均匀分布。

sample_triples.subject: 共轭先验
sample_triples.description: 共轭先验是先验分布的一种特殊类型，其选择可以保证后验分布与先验分布属于同一个分布族，从而极大地简化了后验分布的计算。

sample_triples.subject: 最大后验估计
sample_triples.description: 最大后验估计是一种参数点估计方法，其核心目标是找到使后验分布概率达到最大值的参数点。

sample_triples.subject: 最大后验估计
sample_triples.description: 最大后验估计与最大似然估计是两种紧密相关的参数估计方法。最大后验估计可以看作是最大似然估计的扩展，它在似然的基础上额外考虑了参数的先验分布。当先验分布为均匀分布时，最大后验估计的结果与最大似然估计完全相同。

slices.title: Lect.08
slices.text:
Inner product (1/3)

The standard inner product on $\mathbb{R}^n$ , the set of real n-vectors, is given by

$$\langle x, y \rangle = x^T y = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i, \text{ for } x, y \in \mathbf{R}^n.$$

The Euclidean norm, or $\ell_2$-norm, of a vector $x \in \mathbf{R}^n$ is defined as

$$\|x\|_2 = (x^T x)^{1/2} = (x_1^2 + \dots + x_n^2)^{1/2}.$$
The (unsigned) angle $\alpha \in [0, \pi]$ between nonzero vectors $x, y \in \mathbf{R}^n$ is given by

$$\cos(\alpha) = \frac{\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{y}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|_2 \|\mathbf{y}\|_2}$$

Inner product (2/3)

The standard inner product on $\mathbf{R}^{m \times n}$ , the set of $m \times n$ real matrices, is given by

$$\langle X, Y \rangle = \mathbf{tr}(X^T Y) = \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^n X_{ij} Y_{ij}, \text{ for } X, Y \in \mathbf{R}^{m \times n}$$

Here **tr** denotes trace of a matrix, i.e., the sum of its diagonal elements.

The unit ball of the norm $\|\cdot\|$ : the set of all vectors with norm less than or equal to one,

$$\mathcal{B} = { x \in \mathbf{R}^n \, | \, \|x\| \le 1 }, \quad$$

The $\ell_1$ -norm

The $\ell_1$ -norm is defined as $||x||_1 = |x_1| + \cdots + |x_n|$.

The Chebyshev or $\ell_{\infty}$ -norm

The Chebyshev or $\ell_{\infty}$ -norm is defined as $||x||_{\infty} = \max{|x_1|, \ldots, |x_n|}$.

The $\ell_p$ -norm

The $\ell_p$ -norm, with $p \ge 1$, is defined by $||x||_{p} = (|x_{1}|^{p} + \cdots + |x_{n}|^{p})^{1/p}$.

The $P$-quadratic norms

For $P \in \mathbf{S}_{++}^n$, the $P$-quadratic norms are defined as $||x||_P = (x^T P x)^{1/2} = ||P^{1/2} x||_2$.

Taylor series

The Taylor series of a real or complex-valued function $f(x)$ that is infinitely differentiable at a real or complex number $a$ is the power series:

$$ \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!} (x-a)^n = f(a) + \frac{f'(a)}{1!} (x-a) + \frac{f''(a)}{2!} (x-a)^2 + \cdots $$

A Taylor series expansion of a scalar-valued function of more than one variable can be written compactly as:

$$ f(a) +
abla f(a)^{T}(x-a) + \frac{1}{2!}(x-a)^{T}
abla^{2} f(a)(x-a) + \cdots $$

Use in optimization:

$$ f(x + \Delta x) = f(x) +
abla f(x)^T \Delta x + \frac{1}{2!} \Delta x^T H(x) \Delta x + \cdots $$

where $H(x) = \left[\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i \partial x_i}\right]$ is the Hessian matrix.

Symmetric matrix decomposition

Suppose $A \in \mathbf{S}^n$, i.e., A is a real symmetric $n \times n$ matrix. The spectral decomposition or (symmetric) eigenvalue decomposition of A is

$A = Q \Lambda Q^{T}$,

where $Q \in \mathbf{R}^{n \times n}$ is orthogonal, i.e., satisfies $Q^T Q = I$, and $\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n)$. The (real) numbers $\lambda_i$ are the eigenvalues of A, and are the roots of the characteristic polynomial $\det(sI-A)$. The columns of Q form an orthonormal set of eigenvectors of A.

Symmetric matrix decomposition (2/2)

Assume $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \cdots \geq \lambda_n$. We use the notation $\lambda_i(A)$ to refer to the *i*-th largest eigenvalue of $A \in \mathbf{S}$. We usually write the largest or maximum eigenvalue as $\lambda_1(A) = \lambda_{\max}(A)$, and the least or minimum eigenvalue as $\lambda_n(A) = \lambda_{\min}(A)$. The determinant and trace can be expressed in terms of the eigenvalues,

$\qquad \det(A) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i, \quad \mathrm{Tr}(A) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i,$

as can the spectral and Frobenius norms,

$\qquad \|A\|_{2} = \max_{i=1,...,n} |\lambda_{i}| = \max{\lambda_{1}, -\lambda_{n}}, \quad \|A\|_{F} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_{i}^{2}\right)^{1/2}$

In particular, for any x, we have $\lambda_{\min}(A)x^Tx \leq x^TAx \leq \lambda_{\max}(A)x^Tx$.

Positive definite

A matrix $A \in \mathbf{S}^n$ is called positive definite if for all $x \neq 0, x^T A x > 0$, denoted as $A \succ 0$. We use $\mathbf{S}_{++}^n$ to denote the set of positive definite matrices in $\mathbf{S}^n$.

A matrix $A$ is positive definite if and only if all its eigenvalues are positive, i.e., $\lambda_{\min}(A) > 0$.

If $-A$ is positive definite, we say $A$ is negative definite, which we write as $A \prec 0$.

If $A$ satisfies $x^T A x \ge 0$ for all $x$, we say that $A$ is positive semidefinite or nonnegative definite.

For $A, B \in \mathbf{S}^n$, we use $A \prec B$ to mean $B - A \succ 0$.

Suppose $A \in \mathbf{R}^{m \times n}$ with rank A = r. Then A can be factored as

$$A = U\Sigma V^T$$,

where $U \in \mathbf{R}^{m \times r}$ satisfies $U^T U = I$ , $V \in \mathbf{R}^{n \times r}$ satisfies $V^T V = I$ , and $\Sigma = \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_r)$ , with

$$\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \cdots \ge \sigma_r > 0.$$

The factorization is called the singular value decomposition (SVD) of A. The columns of U are called *left singular vectors* of A, the columns of V are *right singular vectors*, and the numbers $\sigma_i$ are the singular values. The singular value decomposition can be written

$$A = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i u_i v_i^T$$,

where $u_i \in \mathbf{R}^m$ are the left singular vectors, and $v_i \in \mathbf{R}^n$ are the right singular vectors.

SVD and eigendecomposition

The singular value decomposition of a matrix A is closely related to the eigenvalue decomposition of the (symmetric, nonnegative definite) matrix $A^{T}A$. Using (A.12) we can write

$$A^{T}A = V\Sigma^{2}V^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} V & \tilde{V} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \Sigma^{2} & 0 \ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} V & \tilde{V} \end{bmatrix}^{T},$$

where $\tilde{V}$ is any matrix for which $[V \ \tilde{V}]$ is orthogonal. The righthand expression is the eigenvalue decomposition of $A^{T}A$, so we conclude that its nonzero eigenvalues are the singular values of A squared, and the associated eigenvectors of $A^{T}A$ are the right singular vectors of A. A similar analysis of $AA^{T}$ shows that its nonzero eigenvalues are also the squares of the singular values of A, and the associated eigenvectors are the left singular vectors of A.

Lagrange multiplier

Maximize $f(x, y)$ subject to $g(x, y) = 0$.

Lagrange multiplier $\lambda$.

$$\mathcal{L}(x,y,\lambda) = f(x,y) - \lambda \cdot g(x,y)$$

$$
abla_{x,y}f=\lambda
abla_{x,y}g$$

$$
abla_{x,y}f = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right) \quad
abla_{x,y}g = \left(\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\right)$$

As shown in Figure 1, the red line shows the constraint $g(x, y) = c$. The blue lines are contours of $f(x, y)$. The point where the red line tangentially touches a blue contour is the maximum of $f(x, y)$, since $d_1 > d_2$ .

Mean Square Error (MSE)

$J(w) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{t=1}^{N} ||x_t - (x_t^T w)w||^2$

$x_t^T x_t - (x_t^T w) w^T x_t - x_t^T (x_t^T w) w + (x_t^T w) w^T (x_t^T w) w$

$= x_t^T x_t - w^T (x_t x_t^T) w$

Introduce a Lagrange multiplier $\lambda$

$L({\boldsymbol{x}_t}, \boldsymbol{w}) = J({\boldsymbol{x}_t}, \boldsymbol{w}) - \lambda \cdot (\boldsymbol{w}^T \boldsymbol{w} - 1)$

$\frac{\partial J(\boldsymbol{w})}{\partial \boldsymbol{w}} - \lambda \cdot \frac{\partial (\boldsymbol{w}^T \boldsymbol{w} - 1)}{\partial \boldsymbol{w}} = -2(\Sigma_x \boldsymbol{w}) - \lambda \cdot 2\boldsymbol{w} = \boldsymbol{0}$

$\Sigma_x \boldsymbol{w} = (-\lambda) \cdot \boldsymbol{w}$

Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

$\|w\| = 1$

$
\Sigma_x = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{t=1}^N \boldsymbol{x}_t \boldsymbol{x}_t^T$

Applications of PCA

Popular in multivariate statistics, signal processing
Reduce data noise, redundancy, correlation, ...
Dimensionality reduction
Feature selection and feature extraction
Data visualization (to 2D or 3D)

Correlation can be removed by rotating the coordinates to principal components.

$\operatorname{cov}(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)]$

$h_{X,Y} = \frac{\operatorname{cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}$

Signal-noise ratio maximization

Keep one signal dimension, discard one noisy dimension.

Information redundancy

low redundancy

high redundancy

..

Eigen-face method

Sirovich and Kirby (1987) showed that PCA could used on a collection of face images to form a set basis features.

Given input image vector $U \in \mathbb{R}^n$, the mean image vector from the database M, calculate the weight of the kth eigenface as:

$w_k = V_k^T (U - M)$

Then form a weight vector $W = [w_1, w_2, \dots, w_k, \dots, w_n]$.

Compare W with weight vectors $W_m$ of images in the database. Find the Euclidean distance $d = ||W - W_m||^2$.

If $d < \epsilon_1$, then the mth entry in the database is a candidate of recognition.

If $\epsilon_1 < d < \epsilon_2$, then U may be an unknown face and can be added to the database.

If $d > \epsilon_2$, U is not a face image.

slices.title: Lect.09
slices.text:
Inner product

The standard inner product on $\mathbb{R}^n$ , the set of real *n*-vectors, is given by

$$\langle x, y \rangle = x^T y = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i, \text{ for } x, y \in \mathbf{R}^n.$$

The Euclidean norm, or $\ell_2$-norm, of a vector $x \in \mathbf{R}^n$ is defined as

$$\|x\|_2 = (x^T x)^{1/2} = (x_1^2 + \dots + x_n^2)^{1/2}.$$

The (unsigned) angle $\alpha \in [0, \pi]$ between nonzero vectors $x, y \in \mathbf{R}^n$ is given by

$$\cos(\alpha) = \frac{\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{y}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|_2 \|\mathbf{y}\|_2}$$

Inner product (2/3)

The standard inner product on $\mathbf{R}^{m \times n}$, the set of $m \times n$ real matrices, is given by

$$\langle X, Y \rangle = \mathbf{tr}(X^T Y) = \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^n X_{ij} Y_{ij}, \text{ for } X, Y \in \mathbf{R}^{m \times n}$$

Here $\mathbf{tr}$ denotes trace of a matrix, i.e., the sum of its diagonal elements.

The unit ball of the norm $|\cdot|: \mathcal{B} = { x \in \mathbf{R}^n \, | \, \|x\| \le 1 }$.

**Taylor series**

The Taylor series of a real or complex-valued function f(x) that is infinitely differentiable at a real or complex number $a$ is the power series

$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!} (x-a)^n = f(a) + \frac{f'(a)}{1!} (x-a) + \frac{f''(a)}{2!} (x-a)^2 + \cdots$$
A Taylor series expansion of a scalar-valued function of more than one variable can be written compactly as

$$f(a) +
abla f(a)^{T}(x-a) + \frac{1}{2!}(x-a)^{T}
abla^{2} f(a)(x-a) + \cdots$$
Use in optimization:

$$f(x + \Delta x) = f(x) +
abla f(x)^T \Delta x + \frac{1}{2!} \Delta x^T H(x) \Delta x + \cdots$$
where $H(x) = \left[\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i \partial x_i}\right]$ is the Hessian matrix.

Symmetric matrix decomposition (1/2)

Suppose $A \in \mathbf{S}^n$ , i.e., A is a real symmetric $n \times n$ matrix. The spectral decomposition or (symmetric) eigenvalue decomposition of A is

$A = Q \Lambda Q^{T}$,

where $Q \in \mathbf{R}^{n \times n}$ is orthogonal, i.e., satisfies $Q^T Q = I$ , and $\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n)$ . The (real) numbers $\lambda_i$ are the eigenvalues of A, and are the roots of the characteristic polynomial $\det(sI - A)$ . The columns of Q form an orthonormal set of eigenvectors of A.

Symmetric matrix decomposition (2/2)

Assume $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \cdots \geq \lambda_n$. We use the notation $\lambda_i(A)$ to refer to the *i*-th largest eigenvalue of $A \in \mathbf{S}$. We usually write the largest or maximum eigenvalue as $\lambda_1(A) = \lambda_{\max}(A)$, and the least or minimum eigenvalue as $\lambda_n(A) = \lambda_{\min}(A)$. The determinant and trace can be expressed in terms of the eigenvalues,

$$\det(A) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i, \quad Tr(A) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i,$$

as can the spectral and Frobenius norms,

$$\|A\|_{2} = \max_{i=1,...,n} |\lambda_{i}| = \max{\lambda_{1}, -\lambda_{n}}, \quad \|A\|_{F} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_{i}^{2}\right)^{1/2}$$

In particular, for any x, we have $\lambda_{\min}(A)x^Tx \leq x^TAx \leq \lambda_{\max}(A)x^Tx$.

Positive definite

A matrix $A \in \mathbf{S}^n$ is called positive definite if for all $x \neq 0, x^T A x > 0$, denoted as $A \succ 0$. We use $\mathbf{S}_{++}^n$ to denote the set of positive definite matrices in $\mathbf{S}^n$.
A > 0 if and only all its eigenvalues are positive, i.e., $\lambda_{\min}(A) > 0$.
If $-A$ is positive definite, we say $A$ is negative definite, which we write as $A \prec 0$.
If $A$ satisfies $x^T Ax \geq 0$ for all $x$, we say that $A$ is positive semidefinite or nonnegative definite.
For $A, B \in \mathbf{S}^n$, we use $A \prec B$ to mean $B - A \succ 0$.

Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)

Suppose $A \in \mathbf{R}^{m \times n}$ with rank A = r. Then A can be factored as

$$A = U\Sigma V^T,
$$

where $U \in \mathbf{R}^{m \times r}$ satisfies $U^T U = I$ , $V \in \mathbf{R}^{n \times r}$ satisfies $V^T V = I$ , and $\Sigma = \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_r)$ , with

$$\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \cdots \ge \sigma_r > 0.
$$

The factorization is called the singular value decomposition (SVD) of A. The columns of U are called *left singular vectors* of A, the columns of V are *right singular vectors*, and the numbers $\sigma_i$ are the singular values. The singular value decomposition can be written

$$A = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i u_i v_i^T,
$$

where $u_i \in \mathbf{R}^m$ are the left singular vectors, and $v_i \in \mathbf{R}^n$ are the right singular vectors.

SVD and eigendecomposition

The singular value decomposition of a matrix A is closely related to the eigenvalue decomposition of the (symmetric, nonnegative definite) matrix $A^T A$. Using (A.12) we can write

$$A^{T}A = V\Sigma^{2}V^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} V & \tilde{V} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \Sigma^{2} & 0 \ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} V & \tilde{V} \end{bmatrix}^{T},$$

where $\tilde{V}$ is any matrix for which $[V \ \tilde{V}]$ is orthogonal. The righthand expression is the eigenvalue decomposition of $A^T A$, so we conclude that its nonzero eigenvalues are the singular values of A squared, and the associated eigenvectors of $A^T A$ are the right singular vectors of A. A similar analysis of $AA^T$ shows that its nonzero eigenvalues are also the squares of the singular values of A, and the associated eigenvectors are the left singular vectors of A.

Maximize $f(x, y)$ subject to $g(x, y) = 0$.

Lagrange multiplier $\lambda$

$$ \mathcal{L}(x,y,\lambda) = f(x,y) - \lambda \cdot g(x,y) $$

$$
abla_{x,y}f = \lambda
abla_{x,y}g $$

$$

$$

Introduce a Lagrange multiplier $\lambda$

$$L({\boldsymbol{x}_t}, \boldsymbol{w}) = J({\boldsymbol{x}_t}, \boldsymbol{w}) - \lambda \cdot (\boldsymbol{w}^T \boldsymbol{w} - 1)$$

$$\frac{\partial J(\boldsymbol{w})}{\partial \boldsymbol{w}} - \lambda \cdot \frac{\partial (\boldsymbol{w}^T \boldsymbol{w} - 1)}{\partial \boldsymbol{w}} = -2(\Sigma_x \boldsymbol{w}) - \lambda \cdot 2\boldsymbol{w} = \boldsymbol{0}$$

$$\Sigma_x \boldsymbol{w} = (-\lambda) \cdot \boldsymbol{w}$$

Eigen-face method

Sirovich and Kirby (1987) showed that PCA could be used on a collection of face images to form a set of basis features.

Given an input image vector $U \in \mathfrak{R}^n$, the mean image vector from the database is $M$. Calculate the weight of the $k$th eigenface as:

$w_k = V_k^T (U - M)$

Then form a weight vector $W = [w_1, w_2, \dots, w_k, \dots, w_n]$.

Compare $W$ with weight vectors $W_m$ of images in the database. Find the Euclidean distance $d = ||W - W_m||^2$.

If $d < \epsilon_1$, then the $m$th entry in the database is a candidate for recognition.

If $\epsilon_1 < d < \epsilon_2$, then $U$ may be an unknown face and can be added to the database.

If $d > \epsilon_2$, $U$ is not a face image.

What is principle component analysis

1. **Standardization**: The first step in PCA is usually to standardize the data so that each dimension has mean 0 and standard deviation 1. This is important because it treats all variables equally.
2. Covariance Matrix Computation: PCA computes the covariance matrix of the data to understand how the variables in the input data are varying from the mean with respect to each other, or to see if there are any patterns in the variance.
3. Eigenvalue and Eigenvector Calculation: From the covariance matrix, the eigenvalues and eigenvectors are calculated. Eigenvectors determine the directions of the new feature space, and eigenvalues determine their magnitude. In other words, the eigenvectors represent the directions or components for the reduced subspace of the data, whereas the eigenvalues represent the variance of those directions.
4. Sorting and Choosing Principal Components: The eigenvectors are sorted by decreasing eigenvalues. The number of eigenvectors you choose to keep is equal to the number of dimensions you want to reduce your data to. This step involves selecting the top k eigenvectors (where k is the number of dimensions chosen based on the eigenvalue magnitude).
5. **Projection**: Finally, the original data is projected onto the principal component axes to transform the original data into a new set of values, which are the principal components.

PCA is particularly useful in processing data where multicollinearity exists, or when you want to reduce the dimensions of your data by removing the noise and improving interpretability while retaining the essential parts that have more variation. This makes it useful in fields like image processing, genomics, finance, and many areas of science and engineering.

You

Are there any recent applications by principle component analysis?

1. **Financial Sector**: PCA has been adapted for robust factor analysis in financial applications, improving the analysis of large datasets by modifying the traditional PCA method to better handle heavy-tailed data typical in finance. This adaptation, known as Huber PCA, applies a modified loss function to enhance robustness and reduce the impact of outliers.

2. **Biomedical Imaging**: In the field of structured illumination microscopy, PCA is used to enhance image quality by reducing noise and artifacts. This application is particularly valuable for improving the accuracy of sub-pixel measurements in microscopy, which is critical for detailed biological research.

3. Spectroscopy in Medical Diagnosis: PCA has been employed to refine the detection of specific analytes in Raman spectroscopy, aiding medical diagnostics. A variant known as Guided PCA (GPCA) incorporates a reference spectrum to stabilize the analysis across different samples, thus improving the consistency and accuracy of spectroscopic analysis in heterogeneous biological materials.

4. Clinical Medicine: In the clinical setting, PCA has been used to manage and optimize treatment for conditions like congenital adrenal hyperplasia in children. By analyzing a combination of biochemical and clinical markers, PCA helps in stratifying patient profiles to better predict treatment efficacy.

These examples illustrate the versatility of PCA in enhancing data analysis across various high-precision and high-complexity fields.

sample_triples.subject: 负定矩阵
sample_triples.description: 负定矩阵的定义依赖于正定矩阵的概念；具体来说，如果一个矩阵A的相反数-A是正定矩阵，则称该矩阵A为负定矩阵。

sample_triples.subject: 半正定矩阵
sample_triples.description: “半正定矩阵”与“非负定矩阵”在机器学习和线性代数领域中是两个完全等价的术语，用来描述对于所有非零向量x，二次型x^T*A*x均大于等于零的矩阵A。

sample_triples.subject: 左奇异向量
sample_triples.description: 左奇异向量是构成奇异值分解（SVD）的关键组成部分之一，它们是矩阵U的列向量，形成了一组标准正交基。

sample_triples.subject: 右奇异向量
sample_triples.description: 右奇异向量是构成奇异值分解（SVD）的关键组成部分之一，它们是矩阵V的列向量，同样形成了一组标准正交基。

sample_triples.subject: 奇异值
sample_triples.description: 奇异值是构成奇异值分解（SVD）的核心数值元素，它们是对角矩阵Σ的对角线上的非负实数，按降序排列，反映了矩阵在各个奇异向量方向上的“拉伸”程度。

sample_triples.subject: 奇异值分解
sample_triples.description: 奇异值分解与特征值分解之间存在紧密的数学联系。具体而言，对一个矩阵A进行奇异值分解，其左奇异向量是A*A^T的特征向量，右奇异向量是A^T*A的特征向量，而奇异值的平方则是A^T*A（或A*A^T）的非零特征值。

sample_triples.subject: 右奇异向量
sample_triples.description: 矩阵A的右奇异向量与特征向量存在特定关联：它们等同于对称矩阵A^T*A的特征向量。这一关系是连接SVD和特征值分解的桥梁。

sample_triples.subject: 左奇异向量
sample_triples.description: 矩阵A的左奇异向量与特征向量存在特定关联：它们等同于对称矩阵A*A^T的特征向量。

Gaussian distributions
Density function

$$f_{\mathbf{X}}(x_1,\ldots,x_k) = \frac{\exp(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-oldsymbol{\mu})^{\mathrm{T}} \mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-oldsymbol{\mu}))}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^k |\mathbf{\Sigma}|}}$$

Bivariate Gaussian:

In the 2-dimensional nonsingular case ($k=rank(\Sigma)=2$), the probability density function of a vector $x$ is given by:

$$f(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi \sqrt{\det(\Sigma)}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (x-\mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} (x-\mu)\right)$$

where $\mu$ is the mean vector and $\Sigma$ is the covariance matrix.

In the 2-dimensional case, where $x = \begin{pmatrix} x \ y \end{pmatrix}$, the expression simplifies to:

$$f(x,y) = \frac{1}{2\pi \sigma_X\sigma_Y\sqrt{1-\rho^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2(1-\rho^2)}\left[\frac{(x-\mu_X)^2}{\sigma_X^2} + \frac{(y-\mu_Y)^2}{\sigma_Y^2} - \frac{2\rho(x-\mu_X)(y-\mu_Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}\right]\right)$$

where $\rho$ is the correlation between X and Y and where $\sigma_X > 0$ and $\sigma_Y > 0.$ In this case,

$$ \mu = \begin{pmatrix} \mu_X \ \mu_Y \end{pmatrix}, \quad \Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_X^2 & \rho\sigma_X\sigma_Y \ \rho\sigma_X\sigma_Y & \sigma_Y^2 \end{pmatrix}.$$

Conditional Gaussian

If *N*-dimensional **x** is partitioned as follows

$$\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}_1 \ \mathbf{x}_2 \end{bmatrix} \text{ with sizes } \begin{bmatrix} q \times 1 \ (N-q) \times 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

and accordingly $\mu$ and $\Sigma$ are partitioned as follows

$$ \boldsymbol{\mu} = \begin{bmatrix} \boldsymbol{\mu}_1 \ \boldsymbol{\mu}_2 \end{bmatrix} \text{ with sizes } \begin{bmatrix} q \times 1 \ (N-q) \times 1 \end{bmatrix}
 \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \begin{bmatrix} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11} & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21} & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22} \end{bmatrix} \text{ with sizes } \begin{bmatrix} q \times q & q \times (N-q)\ (N-q) \times q & (N-q) \times (N-q) \end{bmatrix}$$

then the distribution of $\mathbf{x}_1$ conditional on $\mathbf{x}_2 = \mathbf{a}$ is multivariate normal ($\mathbf{x}_1 \mid \mathbf{x}_2 = \mathbf{a}$) ~

$$ \mathbf{\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_1 + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1} \left( \mathbf{a} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_2 \right)$$

and covariance matrix

$$ \overline{\mathbf{\Sigma}} = \mathbf{\Sigma}_{11} - \mathbf{\Sigma}_{12} \mathbf{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1} \mathbf{\Sigma}_{21}.$$

Affine transformation

If $\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{B}\mathbf{X}$ is an affine transformation of $\mathbf{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$, where $\mathbf{c}$ is an $M \times 1$ constant vector and $\mathbf{B}$ is a constant $M \times N$ matrix, then $\mathbf{Y}$ has a multivariate normal distribution with expected value $\mathbf{c} + \mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and variance $\mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{T}}$, i.e., $\mathbf{Y} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{c} + \mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{\mu}, \mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{B}^{\mathsf{T}})$.

If $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Lambda} \mathbf{U}^{\mathsf{T}}$ is an eigendecomposition where the columns of $\mathbf{U}$ are eigenvectors and $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$ is a diagonal matrix of the eigenvalues, then we have

$\mathbf{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) \iff \mathbf{X} \sim \boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{U} \boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{1/2} \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{I}) \iff \mathbf{X} \sim \boldsymbol{\mu} +$

An illustration of the generative view

An observed data point $\mathbf{x}$ is generated by first drawing a value $\hat{z}$ for the latent variable from its prior distribution $p(z)$ and then drawing a value for $\mathbf{x}$ from an isotropic Gaussian distribution (illustrated by the red circles) having mean $\mathbf{w}\hat{z} + \boldsymbol{\mu}$ and covariance $\sigma^2 \mathbf{I}$ . The green ellipses show the density contours for the marginal distribution $p(\mathbf{x})$ .

The General EM Algorithm

Given a joint distribution $p(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Z}|\boldsymbol{\theta})$ over observed variables $\mathbf{X}$ and latent variables $\mathbf{Z}$, governed by parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, the goal is to maximize the likelihood function $p(\mathbf{X}|\boldsymbol{\theta})$ with respect to $\boldsymbol{\theta}$.

1. Choose an initial setting for the parameters $\theta^{\text{old}}$.
2. E step: Evaluate $p(\mathbf{Z}|\mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{old}})$.
3. M step: Evaluate $\theta^{\text{new}}$ given by

$$ \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\mathrm{new}} = \arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{Q}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{old}}) $$

where

$$ Q(\theta, \theta^{\text{old}}) = \sum_{\mathbf{Z}} p(\mathbf{Z} | \mathbf{X}, \theta^{\text{old}}) \ln p(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Z} | \theta). $$

4. Check for convergence of either the log likelihood or the parameter values. If the convergence criterion is not satisfied, then let

$$ \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{old}} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\text{new}} $$

and return to step 2.

EM algorithm for FA

E-Step:

$$p^{old}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}) = \frac{G(\mathbf{y}|0,I)G(\mathbf{x}|A\mathbf{y}+\boldsymbol{\mu},\sigma^2 I)}{G(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu},AA^T+\sigma^2 I)}$$

$$E[\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}] = W(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}), \quad W = A^T(AA^T+\sigma^2 I)^{-1}$$

$$E[\mathbf{y}\mathbf{y}^T|\mathbf{x}] = I - WA + W(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^TW^T$$

M-Step:

$$Q(p^{old}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}), \Theta) = \int p^{old}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}) \cdot \ln[G(\mathbf{y}|0, I)G(\mathbf{x}|A\mathbf{y} + \boldsymbol{\mu}, \sigma^2 I)] d\mathbf{y}$$

$$A^{new} = \left(\sum_{t=1}^{N} (\mathbf{x}_t - \boldsymbol{\mu}) (E[\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}_t])^T \right) \left(\sum_{t=1}^{N} E[\mathbf{y}\mathbf{y}^T|\mathbf{x}_t]\right)^{-1}$$

$$\sigma^{2^{new}} = \frac{1}{Nd} \sum_{t=1}^{N} E{(\mathbf{x}_t - A\mathbf{y} - \boldsymbol{\mu})(\mathbf{x}_t - A\mathbf{y} - \boldsymbol{\mu})}$$

Maximum likelihood FA implements PCA

$p(\mathbf{y}) = G(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{0}, I), \quad p(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{y}) = G(\mathbf{x}|A\mathbf{y} + \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_e),$

$p(\mathbf{x}|\Theta) = \int p(\mathbf{y})p(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{y})d\mathbf{y} = G(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}, AA^{T} + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_e),$

$\max_{\Theta} \log \left{ \prod_{t=1}^{N=1} p(\boldsymbol{x}_t | \Theta) \right}$

Maximum Likelihood assume $\boldsymbol{\mu} = \mathbf{0} $ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_e = \sigma_e^2 \mathbf{I}_n$ .

Choosing $m$ by keeping 99% variance $m = \dim(y) = ?$
